title: Connect actions, make requests, and explain choices

grammarPoints.title: Build the verb te-form
grammarPoints.meaning: The te-form connects a verb to later material. Its ending depends on the verb class and, for an う-verb, the final kana. A bare te-form can also be a familiar request.
grammarPoints.formation: る-verbs: drop る + て. う/つ/る → って; む/ぶ/ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. する → して; 来る → 来て（きて）.
notes: 行く is exceptional: 行って. Classify 帰る, 入る, 知る, 要る, 切る, and 走る as う-verbs despite their endings.
The ます stem is not the te-form: 読み becomes 読んで, not 読みて.
Te-forms alone do not specify tense. A bare request is for family or close friends, not a polite request to a stranger.

grammarPoints.title: Make a polite request with てください
grammarPoints.meaning: Ask someone to carry out an action. This is a direct, polite request rather than a question about permission.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb te-form + ください. Keep the particles required by the verb.
notes: Requests should concern actions the listener can intentionally perform.
Do not put ます before ください. A noun request such as 水をください uses the earlier noun pattern.
For close friends, ください can be omitted; in the polite exercises retain it.

grammarPoints.title: Link activities in order
grammarPoints.meaning: Connect actions in a natural sequence. The final verb supplies the tense and politeness for the whole sentence.
grammarPoints.formation: First verb in te-form, then the next verb in its sentence-final form.
notes: と joins nouns, not complete verb predicates.
Keep both actions in the same plausible event sequence; do not choose an unrelated tense for the te-form.
The same link can express how something is done, such as boarding a train and going somewhere. Te-form + すみません can name the cause of an apology.

grammarPoints.title: Give or ask permission with てもいいです
grammarPoints.meaning: Say an action is allowed, or ask whether it is allowed.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb te-form + もいいです; add か for a permission question.
notes: Permission concerns whether an action is acceptable, not whether the speaker has the ability to do it.
A short positive reply can be いいですよ or どうぞ. てもいい cannot stand alone without its verb.
In conversational speech も is sometimes omitted; the full form is てもいいです.

grammarPoints.title: State a prohibition with てはいけません
grammarPoints.meaning: State that an action is forbidden by a rule or by someone in authority.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb te-form + はいけません.
notes: This sounds stronger than a personal request. Use a rule-setting context.
Keep は after the te-form. Do not confuse this with permission or simple present negation.
A gentler personal request using ないでください is introduced in Lesson 8.

grammarPoints.title: Give a reason with から
grammarPoints.meaning: Explain why you made a decision or why a situation holds. At this stage, use an ordinary polite explanation followed by から.
grammarPoints.formation: Situation sentence. Reason sentence + から. A reason can also precede the situation: reason + から、situation.
notes: Keep です or the polite verb before から in these Lesson 6 patterns.
The reason must actually support the decision; random clauses do not make a natural exercise.
The reason-first short-form pattern is developed in Lesson 9.

grammarPoints.title: Offer help with ましょうか
grammarPoints.meaning: Offer to do something that would help the listener. The situation makes it clear that you are offering your own action.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb ます stem + ましょうか.
notes: Unlike a shared suggestion, this means “Shall I…?” in a helping context.
Choose a helpful action that the speaker can perform; do not use it to ask the listener to help.
The speaker is normally omitted. 私が can explicitly identify the person volunteering.
